cases.title: Barishal Coal Plant: Evictions and Assaults at Nishanbaria
cases.place: Khottar Char, Nishanbaria union, Taltali, Barguna, Bangladesh

lenders.name: China Eximbank and Bank of China
lenders.role: China Eximbank and the Beijing and Singapore branches of Bank of China signed a US$427.5 million syndicated loan with Barisal Electric Power Company Ltd in April 2020 for the US$557.89 million plant; Bangladesh's Ministry of Finance gave a sovereign guarantee on 23 December 2020 and a Sinosure insurance policy took effect on 27 October 2021 (AidData). Global Energy Monitor reports that the syndicate issued its first loan in May 2021, completing the financing.

lenders.name: Power Construction Corporation of China (PowerChina), Chinese state-owned (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Owns 96% of Barisal Electric Power Company Ltd (Global Energy Monitor); Iso Tech Group formed the joint venture with Power China Resources in July 2017, and Global Energy Monitor calls it the first power plant invested, built and run by PowerChina in Bangladesh. AidData lists the owners as Barisal Energy (DFC) Holding (92%), Sinohydro (Hong Kong) Holdings (4%) and ISO Tech (4%).

cases.conditions: The loans financed construction of the 350 MW Unit 1 under a 25-year power purchase agreement with the Bangladesh Power Development Board, signed 12 April 2018 (Global Energy Monitor; BWGED).

companies.name: Power Construction Corporation of China (PowerChina)
companies.role: 96% owner of the plant company (Global Energy Monitor); BWGED calls it a sponsor and parent EPC contractor

cases.community: A Bangladesh Working Group on External Debt (BWGED) study found 153 families directly affected by construction, of whom 142 were evicted by force (Global Energy Monitor, citing BWGED). BWGED also records 70 acres of land taken from 20 Rakhine Indigenous families and about 600 affected families of farmers, fishers and Rakhine people in all. In August 2018 villagers petitioned the prime minister, saying the company was buying land through illegal brokers with forged documents; in October 2018 the government said it would investigate (Global Energy Monitor). Transparency International Bangladesh said in February 2019 that the land was government 'khas' land sold by brokers, and that a court injunction on land acquisition had been followed by work resuming with help from the administration and police (The Daily Star).
cases.suppression: Transparency International Bangladesh said local people who filed cases for compensation were being implicated in false extortion cases, threatened and assaulted (The Daily Star, February 2019).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: On 28 September 2020 the National River Conservation Commission ordered the Barguna deputy commissioner to evict the plant for encroaching on Payra River land; PowerChina began building the 217-metre chimney in December 2020 (BWGED). Unit 1 entered commercial operation on 31 December 2022; a second unit was presumed shelved by March 2026 (Global Energy Monitor). In May 2022 Transparency International Bangladesh reported corruption involving the plant (Global Energy Monitor).

cases.title: Zungeru Dam: 98 Communities Displaced and a Court Award

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: Signed a US$984.23 million preferential buyer's credit with the Government of Nigeria on 28 September 2013 for the 700 MW Zungeru hydropower dam (AidData); Daily Trust reported China Exim was to co-finance 75% of the US$1.3 billion project (ICIR).

cases.conditions: The loan financed a US$1.293 billion contract with Chinese state firms CNEEC and Sinohydro, signed 19 October 2012 (AidData).
cases.community: The government's valuation report said 22,100 people, 15,958 farmlands and 6,762 properties in 98 communities would be affected. By January 2015 the compensation committee said about 60% of beneficiaries had been paid, while community leaders said only about half of the more than 20,000 affected people in their districts had been captured for compensation, with payments as low as N9,450; one farmer said he was left with hardly any farmland (ICIR, reporting a Daily Trust investigation). In September 2018 about 700 people who had been moved out of houses taken for the dam, then flooded out, were living in Zungeru Primary School and protested unpaid compensation for their houses (ThisDay). In March 2024 a Niger State High Court accepted the case of 2,845 Samboro community residents that they had been forcibly ejected from their ancestral homes and faced ongoing flooding and erosion from the dam works (Nairametrics).
cases.killed_note: AidData reports that in January 2022 three Chinese workers were abducted after a shootout that killed workers and police; the attackers were not tied to the project, so these deaths are not counted.
cases.outcome: Work stalled in late 2014 and early 2015 after affected communities stopped it over compensation and a court injunction; the minister of state for power reported two to three lawsuits (ICIR). The first 175 MW unit began operating in March 2022 (AidData). On 14 March 2024 Justice Mohammed Mohammed ordered the federal government to pay N1,115,595,047,288 to Abubakar Usman and 2,844 others of Samboro community for destroyed farmland, houses and ponds (Nairametrics).

cases.title: Lahore Orange Line: Homes and Shops Demolished on Short Notice
cases.place: Chauburji and the Orange Line route, Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
cases.point: Orange Line route near Chauburji, where shops were demolished (OpenStreetMap)

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: Signed three loan agreements with the Government of Pakistan on 21 December 2015, including a US$1.235 billion preferential buyer's credit, to pay for the Punjab Mass Transit Authority's contract with CR-NORINCO (AidData).

cases.conditions: The loans financed the April 2015 contract with CR-NORINCO, a consortium of Chinese state firms, for the metro line; civil works began on 25 October 2015 and the project was completed on 8 October 2020 (AidData).

companies.name: CR-NORINCO (China Railway Group and NORINCO consortium)

cases.community: From August 2015 the Lahore Development Authority marked homes, mosques, schools, government buildings and royal tombs for demolition (AidData). On 7 February 2016 The News on Sunday reported that hundreds of families at Kapoorthala House, Jain Mandir and Parachute Colony had been made homeless, shops at Chauburji had been demolished, one resident was given 72 hours to leave, and over 300 affected people gathered at the Lahore High Court over land taken without compensation. Two UN Special Rapporteurs said in January 2016 that residents had been forced out of homes and businesses with little or no notice, in some cases only verbal notice days before demolition. The Lahore Development Authority said Rs5.5 billion had been paid to over 900 people and Rs20 billion set aside for 2,400 affected people, including Rs1 million to each family near Jain Mandir (The Nation).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: The Lahore High Court suspended work near heritage sites in January 2016 and in August 2016 ruled that the government could not evict people or harm heritage sites; in April 2017 the Supreme Court reversed this and allowed construction under 31 conditions (AidData). The first trial run was on 10 December 2019 and the project was completed on 8 October 2020 (AidData).

lenders.name: China Development Bank
lenders.role: Signed a US$3.97 billion loan agreement with the project company PT Kereta Cepat Indonesia China (KCIC) on 14 May 2017 (AidData).

lenders.role: Holds 40% of the project company KCIC; Indonesian state firms hold 60% (AidData).

cases.conditions: The loan financed the 142.3 km line built by KCIC, a joint venture of Indonesian state firms and a consortium of Chinese rail companies led by Beijing Yawan HSR Co. (China Dialogue via Eco-Business).

cases.community: On 22 October 2019 a bored pile driven for the railway hit a Pertamina fuel pipeline in Melong, Cimahi, starting a fire, according to toll road operator Jasa Marga, that killed Li Xuan Feng, a heavy machinery operator for PT Mingshun Construction working on the railway (The Jakarta Post). cases.outcome: The two-week halt lasted until June 2020 because of Covid-19 (China Dialogue). Three lawsuits in July 2018 sought compensation for affected properties (AidData). The line opened on 2 October 2023 (AidData).

cases.place: Cat Linh–Ha Dong line, Hanoi, Vietnam
cases.point: Approximate: Thanh Xuan ward on the line, near the Thanh Xuan site where the November 2014 fatal accident happened

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: Lent a RMB 1.2 billion government concessional loan (October 2008), a US$250 million preferential buyer's credit (November 2009) and a supplementary loan signed in May 2017, about US$669.62 million in all, to Vietnam's Ministry of Finance (AidData).

cases.conditions: Of the initial US$552 million cost, US$419 million came from Chinese loans; the EPC contract went to China Railway Sixth Group, a Chinese state-owned enterprise, and the transport minister said the contract with the Chinese side required Vietnam to buy Chinese-made trains (Vietstock).

companies.name: China Railway Sixth Group (China Railway Group)

cases.community: In November 2014 a crane cable broke at the Thanh Xuan site and a steel rod fell on motorbikes, killing a rider and injuring others (Vietstock, citing Nguoi Lao Dong; VietNamNet). On 28 December 2014 scaffolding and a frame collapsed at the Ha Dong terminal while concrete was poured, damaging a taxi with four people inside and almost killing nine construction workers; no one died (VietNamNet). lenders.role: Own PT Obsidian Stainless Steel 51% and 49% (AidData); OSS refines output from its parent PT Virtue Dragon Nickel Industry in the Morosi industrial area (Mongabay Indonesia).

cases.community: From August 2020 black coal dust from the PT Obsidian Stainless Steel (OSS) power plant spread up to three kilometres into at least six villages of Motui subdistrict (Sama Subur, Wawoluri, Puuwonggia, Ranombopulu, Motui and Lambuluo), entering homes; the Motui village head said children were coughing and having trouble breathing, and 15 village heads signed a written complaint. OSS's mine technical head said the dust came from the company's coal stockpile when it was not watered (Mongabay Indonesia, 2020). In Tani Indah village, the Motui health centre recorded 549 acute respiratory infection patients in 2023 and attributed them to dust exposure; in October 2024 a fish-pond farmer living 200 metres from the OSS power plant lost his milkfish harvest; residents blame hot wastewater from the plant carried into the ponds by a river, and say harvests have fallen from every three months to once a year (Mongabay Indonesia, 2025).

cases.outcome: OSS promised to water its coal and build a covered conveyor (Mongabay Indonesia, 2020). In December 2024 Tani Indah residents, with Walhi Southeast Sulawesi, LBH Kendari and YLBH Makassar, sued OSS and Virtue Dragon at the Unaaha District Court; hearings were under way in March 2025 (Mongabay Indonesia, 2025).

cases.title: Smederevo Steel Mill Under HBIS: Red Dust over Radinac

lenders.name: Bank of China
lenders.role: Extended a US$600 million loan to Hesteel (HBIS) Group in June 2016 for modernising the Smederevo steel mill (AidData).

lenders.name: HBIS Group (Hesteel), Chinese state-owned (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Bought about 98% of the mill's assets from the Serbian state for 46 million euros in April 2016 (AidData; Reuters).

cases.community: Reuters reported in November 2021 that Radinac, a few hundred metres from the furnaces, was covered in thick red dust; a 70-year-old throat cancer patient said residents dry laundry indoors. Smederevo public health data obtained by the group Tvrdjava showed 6,866 cancer cases in 2019 against 1,738 in 2011 in a municipality of about 100,000 people (Reuters). cases.title: Kawama: Homes Bulldozed Beside the Luiswishi Mine
cases.place: Kawama, near Lubumbashi, Haut-Katanga, DR Congo
cases.point: Approximate: Kawama in Ruashi commune, Lubumbashi (OpenStreetMap); a second place named Kawama lies north of the city, and the sources do not give coordinates

lenders.name: Groupe Forrest International (Belgium), through Entreprise Générale Malta Forrest (foreign investor)
lenders.role: EGMF held 60% of the Luiswishi mine through the Compagnie Minière du Sud Katanga (CMSK), a joint venture with state miner Gécamines; the group announced it had sold its CMSK shares in September 2012 (OECD Watch).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the mine.

companies.name: Groupe Forrest International
companies.role: Belgian parent of EGMF, majority owner of CMSK

companies.name: Compagnie Minière du Sud Katanga (CMSK)

cases.community: During a police operation on 24 November 2009 to clear small-scale miners from Kawama, bulldozers belonging to EGMF and driven by its staff destroyed homes and businesses in the three neighbourhoods closest to the Luiswishi mine. Satellite images show 387 structures demolished between 31 May 2009 and 15 May 2010, and videos show permanent brick houses being destroyed while armed police removed villagers, including children (Amnesty International). NGOs put the number of forcibly evicted families at about 500 (OECD Watch, citing ACIDH). Five years later the villagers had received no compensation; one woman whose restaurant was destroyed had to take her children out of school (Amnesty International).
cases.suppression: Armed police removed residents from their homes during the demolitions (Amnesty International). A man shot by mine police had a bullet lodged near his spine removed only after informal arrangements made two years after the NCP case closed (OECD Watch).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: A government prosecutor investigated and tried to bring charges but was told by officials in Kinshasa and the provincial government not to (Amnesty International). The Belgian NCP rejected the case but mediated after the April 2012 complaint, and in its final statement of 12 February 2013 said the process had not improved residents' situation; the company offered water works and a clinic refurbishment through its foundation, which residents rejected (OECD Watch). In November 2014 the Congolese Ministry of Justice told Amnesty it had begun steps to prosecute (Amnesty International).

cases.title: Shell's Vila Carioca Fuel Terminal: Buried Waste and a Contaminated Neighbourhood
cases.place: Vila Carioca, Ipiranga, São Paulo, Brazil
cases.point: Approximate: Vila Carioca neighbourhood, site of Shell's fuel storage terminal

lenders.name: Royal Dutch Shell (Netherlands/UK) through Shell Brasil, with ExxonMobil (US) as minor partner (foreign investors)
lenders.role: Shell Brasil ran the Vila Carioca fuel storage base, open since the 1940s (Consultor Jurídico); ExxonMobil said it was a minor partner in the Brazilian consortium, with Shell as lead partner and facility operator (OECD Watch).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the terminal.

companies.name: Shell (Shell Brasil)
companies.role: Operator of the Vila Carioca terminal

companies.name: ExxonMobil
companies.role: Minor partner in the consortium named in the complaint

cases.community: São Paulo's environment agency Cetesb found that over time the terminal had contaminated soil and groundwater by burying oily sludge and pesticide residues; on 28 May 2002 it recorded fuel odours beyond the site, and a June 2002 survey found 67% of residents interviewed complained of gas, petrol or oil smells, which caused nausea, dizziness and headaches (Consultor Jurídico, citing the federal prosecutor). In January 2005 the government called on Shell and Exxon to stop storing chemicals at and below their facilities and to help workers and residents with high levels of chemicals and heavy metals in their blood (OECD Watch). A São Paulo city council inquiry heard in 2009 that the subsoil and water table were contaminated with lead, pesticides, organochlorines and organophosphates, a problem identified in 1993; at a special health post, 315 of 7,975 possibly exposed people were being monitored, 63 of them with cancer, and no toxicology tests had been done (Câmara Municipal de São Paulo).
cases.killed_note: Residents' association SOS Vila Carioca told the council that Vila Carioca's death rate was 13.9 per 1,000 against 7.8 in Ipiranga (Câmara Municipal de São Paulo); no deaths have been officially tied to the contamination, so none are counted.
cases.outcome: In April 2004 federal prosecutor Sérgio Suiama charged Shell and the National Petroleum Agency with environmental crime, offering to suspend the case if Shell signed a conduct agreement to repair environmental and health damage, which it had refused (Consultor Jurídico). The Brazilian NCP dropped the case against Exxon in 2006 and ended the Shell case on 20 March 2008 after Shell refused mediation, citing court proceedings (OECD Watch). In November 2009 the council inquiry's rapporteur said he would take a complaint against Shell to the human rights commission of the Organization of American States (Câmara Municipal de São Paulo).

cases.title: Aggah: Eni Subsidiary's Oil Roads and Yearly Floods
cases.place: Aggah community, Egbema, Rivers State, Nigeria
cases.point: Approximate: Aggah, beside the Mgbede oil field

lenders.name: Eni S.p.A. (Italy), through Nigerian Agip Oil Company (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Nigerian Agip Oil Company (NAOC), an indirect wholly owned subsidiary of Eni and its Dutch subsidiary Eni International BV, operates the Mgbede oil field that overlaps Aggah (OECD Watch); Eni has operated in the area since the 1970s (LifeGate).

cases.community: Elevated roads and embankments built for oil drilling block the streams that once drained Aggah, causing yearly floods of homes and farmland (OECD Watch). An impact assessment by the complainants found nearly all households had lost crops and more than 65% had suffered physical injuries from the flooding (OECD Watch). cases.outcome: Under Italian NCP mediation, Eni and the complainants agreed on 8 July 2019 that new culverts and drainage channels would be built urgently and existing ones maintained, with a technical expert checking the results; NAOC surveyed the route but work was suspended during Covid-19 (OECD Watch). cases.title: Nidera's Seed Fields at San Pedro: Workers Held in Camps

cases.community: National and Buenos Aires provincial labour inspectors said that in raids in late December 2010 and early January 2011 they found 199 farm workers near San Pedro in conditions close to slavery, 130 of them, including about 30 children and adolescents, working for Nidera; workers could not leave, had no electricity or water, and their cash wages were cut for supplies sold at high prices (All About Feed). Radio Netherlands reported that police found 133 seasonal workers on a Nidera plantation on 30 December 2010, with two holes in the ground as toilets and a pesticide container used as a bath; a San Pedro safety inspector likened the site to a concentration camp. Página/12 reported that two San Pedro farms were raided for alleged reduction to servitude in a court case involving Nidera, and that further joint inspections that week found 274 more workers in exploitative conditions on other companies' fields in Ramallo and Arrecifes.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: Radio Netherlands reported that seven company executives were arrested and Nidera was fined 125,000 euros. Nidera denied the charges (All About Feed). After a complaint by Argentine and Dutch NGOs, Nidera agreed through the Dutch NCP to a human rights policy and due diligence for temporary rural workers; the NCP's final statement of 5 March 2012 confirmed the agreement, and NGO monitoring in the 2011–12 season found conditions satisfactory (OECD Watch).

cases.title: Thervoy Kandigai: Village Commons Cleared for an Industrial Park and Michelin Plant
cases.place: Thervoy Kandigai, Tiruvallur, Tamil Nadu, India

lenders.name: Michelin (France), foreign investor
lenders.role: Acquired land near Thervoy from the Tamil Nadu government in November 2009 and began building what the complaint calls India's largest tyre factory (OECD Watch); its plot covers 117 hectares (French NCP).

cases.conditions: No lender stood above the plant. The state industrial agency SIPCOT acquired the land for the industrial park (Land Conflict Watch).

companies.name: Michelin
companies.role: Tyre factory owner in the SIPCOT industrial park

cases.community: The government took community forest and common grazing land used for decades by Thervoy Kandigai villagers, mostly Dalit and Adivasi families; Land Conflict Watch records 1,200 affected households and 456 hectares. The complaint says 450 hectares of collective forest that supported farming and grazing were destroyed (OECD Watch). The Madras High Court found in September 2009 that SIPCOT had removed 70% of the shrubs and trees despite an order not to fell trees; it ordered 15 families living on the site to be rehoused, which happened in 2013, and ordered the state to set aside 100 acres on the site for fodder crops and give the village 241.86 more acres within three years, by September 2012 (French NCP). The French NCP recognised that Michelin's impact studies were insufficient and that the project had adverse impacts on local people (OECD Watch).
cases.suppression: Villagers leading the protests were charged in false cases and arrested over the years (Land Conflict Watch); the complaint says opposition was severely repressed (OECD Watch).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: The complainants withdrew in September 2013 just before the NCP's final statement, citing its handling of the case (OECD Watch). Michelin carried out a human rights impact study, presented in December 2014, finding the plant's effects strongest in 8 of 31 nearby villages, including Thervoy; the NCP ended its follow-up in February 2016 (French NCP). The pasture land was delayed for years; in 2014, 943 hectares had reportedly been identified at three places, 36 of them at Thervoy (French NCP).

cases.title: Arun III Access Road: Farmers Left Worse Off by Cash-Only Compensation
cases.place: Arun Valley hill route, Sankhuwasabha, Nepal
cases.point: Approximate: Num, in the Arun Valley; the hill road ran along the ridges from Basantapur

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit 2029-NEP of SDR 24.4 million (US$32.8 million), presented to the Board in 1989, financed the access road to the planned Arun III dam (Inspection Panel).

cases.conditions: The credit included a land acquisition, compensation and rehabilitation plan costing US$1.6 million and was meant to build the government's capacity to rehabilitate affected families (Inspection Panel).
cases.community: By July 1990 compensation had been paid to upwards of 40% of an estimated 2,000 families affected by the access road (Inspection Panel, citing an IDA mission). Compensation on the hill route was cash only, with no land, jobs or rehabilitation. A 1991 study for the Bank found many families had spent the cash on debts and subsistence and could not buy new assets; a field survey found recipients had not restored their living standards, as creditors demanded repayment and land prices rose beyond the compensation paid. In 1992 the road was moved to the valley, driving down the value of the land farmers had left. The Panel's report states that farmers on the ridge route suffered substantial damage, first from cash-only compensation and then from the route change; it found about 1,400 other families in a similarly uncertain situation (Inspection Panel).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: On 5 April 1995 the government told the Bank that ridge-route landholders could keep using the land regardless of title, and offered no further help; the Panel found this did not meet the Bank's requirements. The Panel, in its first investigation, issued its report on 21 June 1995 (Inspection Panel).

lvwhy.land: Farmers lost land to the road for cash compensation that left them worse off, then the route was moved (Inspection Panel).

cases.ecosystem: The Panel found that the remaining patches of cloud forest along the abandoned hill route lacked protection measures (Inspection Panel).
